Name: Awdhesh Singh
Question: How do people feel about people who have a lot of money and don't spend it on themselves or their family, but instead save it for the future?
Answer: I am one of those person who always saved money. My saving rate increased with more income because I maintained the same lifestyle despite my higher income, and all my excess income was saved without causing any problems to me. It is due to the habit of saving that I was able to quit my job as an IRS officer at the age of 49, and spending my life doing what I love to do. Let me now explain why I don’t spend more even when I have lots of money. Many of us today earn enough money to eat whatever food we love to eat in any quantity. However, if you are wise, you know that you need only around 2400 calories per day to live a healthy life. You also know that if you eat a lot of food, you may end up consuming 5000–10000 calories per day, and the excess food and calories, instead of nourishing you, will become the source of your obesity and numerous diseases like diabetes, blood pressure, cardiac problems etc. Hence, if you eat less, only what is needed by the body, despite your financial status, you are demonstrating that you have full control over your body and mind and you are not a seeker of pleasure that destroys your body, mind and soul. It is a fact that the best things in life are quite affordable, while harmful things are very expensive. Today I can afford to eat the best food in the best hotel, but I rarely go there because whenever I go there I not only have to spend huge money for dining, but I also end up consuming double the calories, and it takes a week of pain and exercise to shed those extra calories to maintain my weight. Oscar Wilde once said— 'Nowadays people know the price of everything and the value of nothing.' If you understand the value of the thing, you don’t have to spend lots of money to enjoy life. Pat Williams, beautifully said, “Money can buy a house, but not a home; a bed, but not rest; food, but not an appetite; medicine, but not health; information, but not wisdom; thrills, but not joy; associates, but not friends; servants, but not loyalty; flattery, but not respect.” When the most valuable things in the world are free, why should we spend money buying useless things and waste our lives earning that useless money? Question: Why does Awadhesh Singh (respected), in most of his answer mention about his self achievement like IIT, ex-IRS, PhD, etc.? How can such a genius, intellectual, and rational person be obsessed with self praise?
Answer: We all have to provide our credentials with our bio on Quora. According to Quora, we must give our credentials because “Credentials add credibility to your content”. Thus, I don’t self-praise myself but only show my credentials to help people know who I am, and how hard I have worked to reach my present position. Furthermore, my credentials are spread over four decades, which shows that I have not stopped growing even when I am nearing sixty. My life has been a struggle to grow more and become a better version of myself. A well-known quote by Gina Milicia reads, “A comfort zone is a beautiful place, but nothing ever grows there.” I had the choice to live a comfortable life as an IRS officer, but I instead chose difficulty to make my life worthwhile and interesting through intellectual growth. I firmly believe in the saying “You don’t grow old. You become old when you stop growing.” I hope to achieve many more milestones in life and add many new credentials to my bio. And, I wish to share all my knowledge and wisdom acquired through years of effort freely to the world. Hence, I intend to remain young forever by keep growing till the last day of my life. Question: If you had to change one thing you did in the past, what would it be and why did you pick it?
Answer: That is a very interesting question. I usually don’t think about changing my past because it is simply impossible. But assuming I can do it, let me try to answer this question. When I was in class 12th (1983), I had no idea of the IIT-JEE examination, as no one in my family was an engineer. However, I had a friend named Alok Mathur, whose father was a Gold Medalist from Roorkee University (now IIT-Roorkee), and his two elder brothers were in IIT Kanpur. He joined postal coaching of Agrawal Classes and suggested to me that I should share the course and the fee (which was Rs 600 then, so I had to pay Rs 300 to share the course). In those days, I was against the idea of coaching, so I refused. The result was that though we used to score similar marks in school, he got into IIT Kanpur with a 322 rank, while I got IT-BHU Varanasi with a 1331 rank. So, perhaps I should have accepted his advice and joined Agrawal Classes. On second thought, I feel that I should not have gone to IIT or done Mechanical Engineering at all because, after four years, I was going to write UPSC civil services. Please permit me to change my action once. My optionals for civil services were mathematics and physics, which I had to study from scratch, and I wasted my four years studying mechanical engineering. How good it would have been if I had instead chosen BSc course followed by M Sc, and spent four years studying Mathematics and Physics. I am sure that if I had done B Sc, I would have got the top rank in the civil services examination and perhaps been selected for IAS with the top rank, and got home cadre. But then, what was the use of becoming an IAS if, after a decade, I was to do the PhD, and quit the civil services to become a writer? I would have quit IAS anyway. So, it seems that I wasted 25 years of my life in civil services, and today, I am not using anything I learned in civil services. Please permit me to change the ‘one thing’ once again. I should have joined PhD after my M Tech and become a professor in some prestigious college. Perhaps I would have published thousands of research papers and written dozens of books by now. However, all my books would have been on technical subjects, which would have been read by a few thousand people. That would have been worse than what I am doing today. I think I have to change my one thing once again. Oh! I am so confused. I accept that I have not made the best decisions in my life. However, if I had made better decisions (from today’s perspective), as I discussed above, I would have perhaps missed many things in life, like: Hence, finally, I decided not to change anything I did in the past because everything I have done in my life has given me unique and beautiful experiences, and added lustre to my life. What I am today is due to the experiences of my life. If I change anything of the past, I will no longer be the same person as I am now. Since I love my life today and enjoy every moment of my life, I would not like to opt for a different life by changing anything that I did in the past.

Question: How has the Narendra Modi government reduced corruption in India?
Answer: It is a myth that corruption is reducing under the Modi government. As a matter of fact, corruption has continuously increased since the Modi government came to power in 2014. It is evident from the report of German-based Transparency International, an international agency to assess corruption in different countries in the world, that India’s ranking is getting worse after 2015. While India was continuously improving its ranking before 2014–2015 and rose from ranking 94 to 76, since 2015, it has been decreasing and now in 2023, it is 93. [1] Similarly, India is the worst Asian country according to the citizen survey of corruption in India and select Asian countries according to a report in 2020 where 39% of the citizens accepted to have paid bribes to government officers, worse than any other Asian country surveyed. [2] What the Modi government has done is to make the anti-corruption agencies powerless by amending Section 17A of the Prevention of Corruption Act in 2018 so that now the officers of CBI or other agencies can’t even start corruption cases against the government employees without the permission of the Government.[3] Further, governments are now appointing only loyal officers, who, instead of following the law books, would never make any case against the government, and only target the opposition. As a result, you don’t hear cases of corruption booked against government officers and ministers nowadays, though corruption is increasing every year under the present regime. However, most people in India have become so blind due to their faith, that they will ignore every evidence against their Supreme leader whom they consider nothing less than God’s incarnation in Kaliyoga.

Question: What is your review of 12th Fail movie and the hype around it?
Answer: I watched the Hindi movie 12th Fail a few days ago on the OTT platform. I liked the movie but not the message that the movie tries to convey. Let me now explain why I disagree with the message. The Civil Services Examination is certainly one of the toughest examinations in the world with a rejection rate of over 99.9% (less than 1000 people get selected among one million applicants). It is perhaps the only examination in the world that can transform your life forever, and ensure you high status and lifetime job security. However, it is also a fact that you must be really a brilliant student to succeed in the examination. In this movie, a 12th failed student Manoj Kumar Sharma, who came from a very poor family background get selected into the Indian Police Service (IPS), in his last attempt, presumably at the age of 33 years since the maximum age for the general category candidate is 32 years. Here is the picture of real and reel life Manoj Sharma.[1] Imagine, if he was not selected for the civil services examination in the last attempt. What type of job he would have got, or career choices he would have? Should we encourage young people to spend a decade of their life to realise their dream of becoming a top civil servant? Does IAS/IPS/IFS/IRS are really worth the hype created in the movie? Unfortunately, every year, lakhs of students fail to make it to the civil services examination after almost a decade of effort motivated by such stories of exceptional success and ruin of their youth and life. The key message of the movie is that if a 12th fail can get selected into civil services, anyone can get selected. This message is wrong because your academic track record plays a very important role in your success in all competitive examinations, including CSE. I, for example, was selected for the civil services examination (IRS) in the first attempt itself in 1990, while doing my M-Tech at IIT Delhi. And I was not an exception. In those days more than 100 students (among 700 odd selections) were selected from IIT Delhi alone with hardly 400 students who appeared in the examination. If my memory serves me right, there were almost 15 ranks in the CSE from IIT in the top 20 in the year 1990 selection, most of them in their very first attempt. Thus the success percentage in IIT Delhi was more than 25% on those days, as against the overall success rate of less than 0.5%. Further, the maximum age for appearing in CSE in those days was only 26 years for the general category. Hence, the risk of taking civil services was minimal for IIT students as even those who failed to make it, could easily get jobs in academic or corporate. It is thus evident that academic brilliance plays a significant role in achieving success in CSE, and a brilliant student has at least 100 times more chance of selection than a 12th Fail sudent. Hence, if you have a poor track record in academics, you must understand that you are taking a huge risk by taking the civil services examination if you don’t have a backup option. If anyone collects the data of selection, I am sure it can be easily established that most people who get selected have consistently good academic records while most candidates with poor records may fail to even clear the Prelims in all their attempts. While the 12th Fail movie will motivate hundreds of thousands of young students to dedicate a decade of their lives to become a top civil servant, more than 99% per cent of them would repent their decision after a decade and ruin their lives. I am not discouraging the academically poor students from writing the CSE, but they must realistically evaluate their chances of success before attempting the examination. .
